resident.chief_complaint: Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months in a 41-year-old female with no history of trauma.
resident.history: A 41-year-old female with no history of trauma presented with weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months. Initial cervical noncontrast MRI showed a hyperintense intramedullary cord signal, with differential diagnoses including cervical spondylotic myelopathy and tumor. She was referred for an open biopsy of the cervical spinal cord to document the pathology of the tumor. At the time of transfer, she had severe spastic quadriparesis, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Follow-up MRI revealed cervical spondylosis with C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression associated with an extensive intramedullary high cord signal and cord enlargement on T2-weighted sagittal images extending from C5 to C7; axial images confirmed the intramedullary signal abnormality. T1-weighted MRI sagittal scan showed the lesion enhanced with contrast at the C5–C6 level.
resident.physical_exam: On examination at the time of transfer, severe spastic quadriparesis was present, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction were reported in the history. Detailed motor power, reflexes, sensation, and sphincter examination findings are not documented in the record.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord lesion at C5–C7, likely intramedullary, producing upper motor neuron signs in all four limbs. The upper extremity predominance suggests central cord involvement. Detailed motor, reflex, sensory, and sphincter examination findings are not documented, limiting precise localization.

red_flags.finding: Intramedullary cord enlargement and contrast enhancement at C5–C6 on MRI
red_flags.rationale: This suggests an intrinsic cord lesion (e.g., tumor, demyelination, inflammation) that could independently cause the progressive myelopathy; surgical decompression for spondylotic compression may not address the primary pathology, and biopsy or medical management may be needed.

In compressive cervical myelopathy from C5–C7 spondylosis, lower extremities are typically more affected due to longer corticospinal tracts; upper extremity predominance suggests a central cord or intramedullary process, reinforcing the likelihood of a primary cord lesion rather than compression alone.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The imaging shows C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression, but the clinical pattern of upper extremity-predominant spastic quadriparesis is atypical for compressive cervical myelopathy at those levels, which would be expected to affect lower limbs more; additionally, cord enlargement and contrast enhancement are not typical for simple spondylotic compression, suggesting an intramedullary lesion that better explains the symptoms.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of intensive conservative therapy.
New or worsening neurological deficits at any point during the conservative trial.
Progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or contrast enhancement on follow-up cervical MRI at 3 months.
Inability to participate in therapy due to pain, functional decline, or medical instability.
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I remain the strongest advocate for conservative care. Given the progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, surgery is being considered, but before proceeding to irreversible intervention, I propose a formal, time-limited 3-6 month trial of intensive conservative management under close neurological monitoring. This would include supervised physical therapy for gait/balance/strength, occupational therapy for activities of daily living, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, and avoidance of high-risk activities. The literature on nonoperative management of cervical spondylotic myelopathy reports that a subset of patients—particularly those with mild symptoms and no rapid progression—can stabilize or improve without surgery; however, I acknowledge that severe spastic quadriparesis with sphincter involvement and cord enhancement indicates a poorer prognosis for conservative care. Therefore, I define failure as any of the following: (1) no improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of strict conservative therapy; (2) new or worsening neurological deficits during the trial; (3) progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or enhancement on follow-up MRI at 3 months; or (4) inability to participate in therapy due to pain or functional decline. If any of these occur, I will accept that conservative management has failed and support surgical intervention or biopsy as appropriate. Until then, I hold my stance for a trial of conservative care.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Deputy Director points to progressive sphincter dysfunction and an enhancing intramedullary lesion as reasons to avoid delay, arguing that waiting risks irreversible damage. I have already incorporated these findings into my failure criteria: any new or worsening neurological deficit during the trial triggers immediate surgical consideration, and lack of improvement at 3 months ends the conservative attempt. Under this protocol, the risk of irreversible damage from waiting is minimized, because we will not hesitate to intervene at the first sign of deterioration. The enhancing lesion does not mandate urgent surgery; it mandates close surveillance and a short, time-limited trial with a low threshold for crossover. I therefore maintain my stance for a structured conservative trial with defined stopping rules.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 41-year-old woman with a 2-month history of progressive quadriparesis (upper greater than lower) and sphincter dysfunction. MRI shows cervical spondylotic compression at C5-6 and C6-7 with extensive T2 cord signal and enlargement from C5 to C7 and focal enhancement at C5-6. The clinical severity and rapid progression indicate severe myelopathy requiring urgent intervention. However, the cord enlargement and contrast enhancement are not typical for pure spondylotic myelopathy and raise concern for intrinsic cord pathology such as tumor, demyelination, or inflammation. A 3-6 month trial of conservative care is not justified given the risk of irreversible deficit; any observation should be very short and closely monitored. Definitive management should address both cord compression and obtain tissue diagnosis unless rapid workup strongly suggests a medical cause.
proposed_options: Urgent posterior cervical decompression (C5-7 laminectomy or laminoplasty) with intraoperative dural opening and biopsy of the enhancing intramedullary lesion; this addresses compressive myelopathy and provides tissue diagnosis in one setting.
Anterior cervical decompression and fusion at C5-6 and C6-7 for the compressive component, with staged posterior biopsy if the enhancing lesion persists or progresses postoperatively.

Short-course aggressive medical/inflammatory workup (CSF analysis, serum AQP4/MOG/oligoclonal bands, infectious and rheumatologic panels, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) and possible high-dose corticosteroids if demyelinating disease is suspected, with repeat MRI in 1-2 weeks; proceed to surgery if no improvement or diagnosis remains unclear.

Immediate biopsy via laminectomy without formal decompression, if the compressive component is judged not to be the dominant cause; this establishes diagnosis but may delay decompression of an already compromised cord.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Urgent posterior decompression with biopsy (Option 1), provided a rapid inflammatory workup does not reveal a clear medical cause; otherwise, medical management first.
disagreement_points: The physiatrist's 3-6 month conservative trial is not acceptable for this degree of myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction; such delay risks permanent loss of function. Any conservative window should be measured in days, not months.

There is uncertainty whether the cord enlargement and enhancement represent primary intramedullary pathology (tumor, inflammation) or reactive change to compression. This changes the surgical plan and the role of biopsy.

Immediate decompression without tissue diagnosis may be inadequate if an intrinsic tumor is present; conversely, biopsy without decompression may worsen neurological status by surgical manipulation in an already compromised cord.

The lack of documented past medical history, laboratory data, and detailed neurological timeline limits our ability to exclude rapidly progressive demyelinating disease, which would be treated medically, not surgically.
deferred_questions_to_director: Can we obtain prior imaging, outside records, and any laboratory results before proceeding? This includes inflammatory markers, CSF studies if done, and history of recent infection or vaccination.
Does the director prefer anterior, posterior, or combined approach for decompression given the need for possible biopsy?
Is there a neuropathologist available for intraoperative frozen section if biopsy is taken?
Should we obtain a CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or spinal angiogram to rule out systemic disease or vascular malformation before surgery?
vice_opinions.public_message: My assessment is that this patient has severe progressive cervical myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction and imaging showing both compression and an enhancing intramedullary lesion. I would not wait 3-6 months for conservative therapy; that risks irreversible damage. I recommend urgent surgical intervention that includes decompression and biopsy to address both possible causes. However, before final decision, we should rapidly rule out inflammatory/demyelinating disease. I defer the final operative plan to you.

director_rulings.final_decision: Proceed with urgent diagnostic workup before operative intervention. Obtain prior records, serum and CSF studies, and complete imaging to rule out demyelinating/inflammatory or systemic disease. If workup identifies a medical cause, treat medically and defer surgery. If no medical cause is found, proceed with urgent posterior cervical decompression with biopsy of the enhancing intramedullary lesion. The physiatrist's 3-6 month conservative trial is rejected; any nonoperative window is limited to the time needed for this workup (24-48 hours).
delegated_tasks: Resident: obtain all prior medical records, including previous imaging, laboratory results, and detailed history, especially recent infections, vaccinations, or autoimmune symptoms.
Neurologist: advise on the most appropriate rapid inflammatory/demyelinating workup and interpret results in the context of the enhancing lesion.
Radiologist: review outside imaging if available and perform the ordered MRI/CT sequences; provide detailed report including enhancement pattern, cord expansion, and any additional lesions.
Anesthesiologist: perform preoperative assessment including airway evaluation and optimize for potential surgery.
Vice_director: coordinate the operating room and neuropathology availability for possible intraoperative frozen section.
